newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Aborigine cleared of death curse extortion.
newsitem.headline: Aborigine cleared of death curse extortion.

text.p: An Australian court on Thursday acquitted an Aborigine charged with trying to extort A$10,000 (US$7,600) by threatening to "point the bone", or place a death curse, on an Australian comedian.

Northern Territory Supreme Court Judge Steven Bailey directed a jury to acquit Aboriginal activist John Kelly, and his manager, after finding the men had no case to answer after a three-day trial in the northern city of Darwin.
Kelly, 50, and Darwin bookmaker Bryan Clark, 45, were charged with making a demand with menaces.
Judge Bailey said there was no evidence of unlawful conduct and that it was "everyday practice" for offers to be made to "buy off unfavourable politically adverse publicity".
Outside the court, Kelly said he would temporarily stop putting curses on people.
"I am going to let that rest for the time being, that is a thing which almost got me into trouble," Kelly told reporters.

The court heard that Kelly had threatened to put a death curse on comedian Kevin Wilson after he heard Wilson perform a song which contained the words "boong" and "coon" in 1994, claiming Wilson was making jokes at the expense of Aborigines, the court heard during the trial.
Both words are derogatory terms for Aborigines.
Kelly's manager later telephoned Wilson's manager and initially asked for a new four wheel drive vehicle, but later dropped the demand to A$10,000, the court heard.
In a telephone conversation taped at the time, transcripts of which were tendered in court, Wilson's manager asked Clark: "If you get the money you won't point the bone at Kevin?"
"No pointing the bone, yeah," Clark replied.
